senses.definition: (obsolete except in set terms) Having the same mother and father; a full (brother or sister).
(obsolete except in set terms) Being born to one’s blood aunt or uncle, a first (cousin).

quotes.text:
The doubtfull wordes whereof they scan and canvas to an fro.
Which done, Prometheus sonne began by counsell wise and sage
quotes.reference: 1567 Arthur Golding trans., Ovid's Metamorphoses, Book 1, lines 460-2

quotes.text: After this Merlyn told vnto kynge Arthur of the prophecye / that there shold be a grete batail besyde Salysbury and Mordred his owne sone sholde be ageynste hym / Also he tolde hym that Basdemegus was his cosyn and germayn vnto kynge Vryence
quotes.reference: 1485, Sir Thomas Malory, “xj”, in Le Morte Darthur, book II:

quotes.text: The phrase would bee more Germaine.
quotes.reference: c. 1599–1602 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Tragedie of Hamlet, Prince of Denmarke”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London: […] Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act V, scene ii]:

quotes.text: Wert thou a Leopard, thou wert Germane to the Lion.
quotes.reference: c. 1605–1608 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Life of Tymon of Athens”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London: […] Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act IV, scene iii]:

quotes.text: Which when his german saw, the stony feare / Ran to his hart, and all his sence dismayd […]
quotes.reference: 1590, Edmund Spenser, “Book II, Canto VIII”, in The Faerie Queene. […], London: […] [John Wolfe] for William Ponsonbie, →OCLC:

senses.definition: An elaborate round dance, often with a waltz movement.

quotes.text: Through the years, though, the german was replaced by new and more popular dances, but in many instances the name stayed on.
quotes.reference: 1985, Betty Casey, Dance Across Texas, page 49:

senses.definition: A social party at which the german is danced.
